newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH - We've had our monetary Christmas present.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH - We've had our monetary Christmas present.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello seems to have ruled out what little chance there was of a third monetary easing for this year.
This afternoon he was asked at a doorstop news conference at Parliament House whether business should have another rate cut.
He responded first by describing any further easing as something to talk about next year.
Then he said the past rate cuts should be allowed to have their effect on the economy -- by implication, before any further movement.
After that, perhaps suspecting he had given away too much, he obfuscated, in the time-honoured tradition of treasurers talking about monetary policy.
Here is the revealing first part of his answer, answering a question from ABC reporter Lyndal Curtis.
"Well, there've already been two cuts in official interest rates since our government came to office.
"You know, you want to think about this year's Christmas present before you start talking about next year's, Lyndal.
"This has been a very good result. Let's just let those interest rates work themselves into the economic system."
And then he obfuscated.
A SOFT-SHOE SHUFFLE

One of the delights of listening closely to every government statement on the economy (yes, there are some) is noticing the little verbal shuffles as they try to drop forecasts that are becoming embarrassments.
At the moment the most seriously dubious budget economic forecasts are those for the labour force.
Today, both Costello and his new assistant treasurer, Rod Kemp, said that the two percent employment growth forecast was looking good.
Well, actually there are two employment growth forecasts, and one that says two percent is the through-year figure (that is, the change between the June quarters of 1995 and 1996).
The 1.5 percent year-average forecast is no longer being mentioned by the ministers, presumably because it probably won't be delivered by the 1997 upturn on which the government is relying.
(It's hard to hit a year-average target if you get off to a late start).
The emphasis on the through-year number is almost a silent admission that the year-average one won't be met.
Costello was specifically asked about the year-average forecast today. He obfuscated.
AND THE MID-YEAR REVIEW will be early next year, Costello said today.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
